title: U.S. House · Alabama's 3rd Congressional District
area: East-central Alabama, including Anniston, Auburn, Opelika, and Phenix City along the Georgia border.

context.text: Incumbent Mike Rogers (R) defeated Terri LaPoint 83.2% to 16.8% in the May 19, 2026 Republican primary; Lee McInnis advanced from the Democratic primary unopposed. Cook Political Report rated the district R+23 for 2026.

candidates.name: Mike Rogers
candidates.ballotNote: Won the May 19, 2026 Republican primary, 83.2% to 16.8%, over Terri LaPoint.
candidates.currentRole: U.S. Representative for Alabama's 3rd Congressional District (since 2003)

summary.text: Mike Rogers is the incumbent Republican U.S. Representative for Alabama's 3rd Congressional District, first elected in 2002. A Calhoun County attorney and small-business owner, he served on the Calhoun County Commission and in the Alabama House of Representatives, including as minority leader, before entering Congress. He chairs the House Committee on Armed Services in the 119th Congress and is seeking another term.

background.text: Born in Hammond, Indiana, in 1958. His official biography describes him as a sixth-generation East Alabamian who grew up in the mill village of Blue Mountain in Calhoun County, where his mother worked in a textile mill and his father was a firefighter.

Graduated from Saks High School, then earned bachelor's (political science, 1981) and Master of Public Administration (1984) degrees from Jacksonville State University and a J.D. from the Birmingham School of Law (1991), where his official biography says he graduated with honors.
Was previously a practicing attorney and small-business owner in Calhoun County, according to his official biography.
Served on the Calhoun County Commission from 1987 to 1990; at age 28 he was the youngest person to join it, according to Wikipedia.
Served in the Alabama House of Representatives from 1994 to 2002, as minority leader from 1998 to 2000.
Elected to the U.S. House in 2002 to succeed Bob Riley, who was elected governor; he defeated Democrat Joe Turnham 50% to 48%, according to Wikipedia.
Chairs the House Armed Services Committee, and served as ranking member of the Committee on Homeland Security in the 116th Congress, according to his official biography.

His official biography says that while on Armed Services he initiated and oversaw the creation of the U.S. Space Force, and that his district is home to the Anniston Army Depot and the Fort Benning community. Wikipedia reports that a 2017 Space Corps proposal he worked on with Rep. Jim Cooper passed the House but not the Senate, and that similar language was enacted two years later.
According to his official biography, he is married to his wife Beth and is the father of three.

priorities.text: On announcing his 2026 campaign, said Congress must close the border, protect the unborn, expand domestic energy production, and grow the economy, building on the agenda pursued under President Trump.

positions.summary: Cosponsored H.R. 722, the Life at Conception Act, a bill to implement equal protection under the 14th Amendment for the right to life of each born and preborn human person.
Cosponsored H.R. 38, the Constitutional Concealed Carry Reciprocity Act of 2025, a bill allowing nonresidents of a state to carry concealed firearms there if their home state permits it.

record.text: Chairs the House Committee on Armed Services in the 119th Congress (2025-2026).
Served as Ranking Member of the House Committee on Armed Services in the 117th Congress (2021-2022).
Served as Ranking Member of the House Committee on Homeland Security in the 116th Congress (2019-2020).

candidates.researchNotes: Rogers has not completed a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey. His official House site's 15 issue subpages (Agriculture, Budget, Economy, Health, Homeland Security, International Relations, Taxes, etc.) each display only "More text to come!" with no substantive text of his own, and the linked press releases under most of them date from 2011-2018 and are too old and general to document a current position; his campaign site (mikerogersforcongress.com) has no issues page beyond a single brief 2026 campaign-launch quote (used above as a priority) and general biography. No issue-specific position was found that directly and specifically addresses any of the 15 guide issue statements, so none is documented; this is left as an honest gap rather than inferred from party or rhetoric.

candidates.name: Lee McInnis
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the Democratic primary unopposed.

summary.text: Lee McInnis is a retired U.S. Army veteran and Defense Intelligence Community officer and the Democratic nominee for Alabama's 3rd Congressional District. An Alabama native and Auburn University graduate, he served in the Army as an Arabic linguist, worked 28 years in defense intelligence, and later taught at the college level. He has not previously held elected office; his campaign emphasizes health care access in rural Alabama, education, affordability, fair taxes and veterans' care.

background.text: Born in Birmingham and raised in Homewood, Alabama; graduated from Homewood High School.
Earned a bachelor's degree (1983) from Auburn University, then, after Army service using the GI Bill, a master's degree (1987) studying communications and international relations.
Served in the U.S. Army from 1983 to 1989, trained as an Arabic linguist.

Spent a 28-year career in the Defense Intelligence Community, with extended time overseas in Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq, and Afghanistan; he reports receiving the Joint Staff Civilian Commendation Medal and the Defense Intelligence Agency's Director Intelligence Medal. Describes his work as including serving as an intelligence officer and lead instructor.
Describes retiring when his wife's job moved the family to Augusta, Georgia, and taking a job teaching at a local college; the couple later settled in Lee County, where he lives in Opelika.
Returned to Auburn University and earned a master's degree in history in 2024.
Announced his candidacy at the Opelika Public Library in late 2025; he has no prior campaigns or offices listed. Advanced from the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary.
Is affiliated with Indivisible Auburn/Opelika, the NAACP (Branch 5038), Auburn United Methodist Church, the National Eagle Scout Association, and the American Legion.

priorities.text: Health care: says Republican budget cuts to Medicaid and health spending threaten rural hospitals, citing an estimate that Alabama could lose 20 rural hospitals and 200,000 to 500,000 residents' health coverage.
priorities.quote: 83% of Alabama's rural hospitals are running at a financial loss.

priorities.text: Education: says he opposes what he calls a "two tier" education system and supports revitalizing technical education and making college more affordable.
Economy and tariffs: says tariffs are raising prices and hurting farmers in the district, and that the country must build an economy that "lifts all people."

positions.summary: Says the ultra-rich and large corporations should pay a fair share of taxes, and that working and middle-class Americans have carried too much of the tax burden.
positions.quote: Make sure the ultra-rich and corporations pay their fair share.

positions.summary: Says tariffs are causing rising prices and job losses and hurting farmers in his district.
positions.quote: Already tariffs are causing rising prices and job loses.

positions.summary: At a November 2025 town hall, described current immigration enforcement as illegal, unconstitutional and inhumane, per The Auburn Plainsman.

statements.quote: We talk about how everybody in this district should have an equal shot at having a healthy life, and that includes healthcare, that includes clean water, that includes universal lunches for school children
statements.context: In an Alabama Reflector interview, October 2026

candidates.researchNotes: No campaign website was found. Added statements and positions come from Alabama Reflector (Oct. 2026) and The Auburn Plainsman (Nov. 2025 town hall). The Plainsman reports he pledged red flag laws and an assault-weapons ban but quotes nothing from him, so no gun position is recorded. His living-wage remarks do not mention the minimum wage.
